Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Its **root datum** is the quadruple
$$R(G,T)=(X(T),\Phi(G,T),X_*(T),\Phi^\vee(G,T)),$$
where the character and cocharacter lattices are those of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]], the roots are the nonzero adjoint characters, and $\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee:\alpha\in\Phi\}$ consists of the associated coroots. Its **rank** is $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}X(T)=\dim T$. For a split Borel pair $(B,T)$, its base $\Delta(B)$ consists of roots in $\Phi^+(B)$ that are not sums of two positive roots; the pair gives the based root datum $(R(G,T),\Delta(B))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the root-group, Weyl and centre suppliers for the following structural assertions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The coroots supplied by [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]] are in bijection with the roots and satisfy $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. This quadruple is a reduced root datum in the sense of [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]], its Weyl group is canonically $W(G,T)$, and $\Delta(B)$ is a base whose nonnegative integral combinations recover $\Phi^+(B)$ ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). Its semisimple rank is $|\Delta|=\operatorname{rank}G-\dim Z(G)$, and $G$ is semisimple exactly when $\mathbb Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X(T)$ ([[lem-reductive-center-radical-and-semisimple-quotient]]).

The isomorphism class of the unbased root datum is independent of the split Borel pair, but it is not asserted to have a unique abstract isomorphism: Weyl automorphisms already refute that assertion in type $A_1$. For two fixed split Borel pairs $(B,T),(B',T')$, conjugation by $g\in G(k)$ carrying the first pair to the second induces a canonical comparison of their **based** root data. If $g'$ is another such element, $g^{-1}g'$ lies in $N_G(B)\cap N_G(T)=B\cap N_G(T)=T$, by Borel self-normality and the Weyl/Borel correspondence. Conjugation by $T$ acts trivially on its character and cocharacter lattices and preserves the root-coroot labels, so the two induced comparisons agree. Thus uniqueness applies to the comparison attached to the fixed based pairs, while the unbased datum is defined up to isomorphism class. Then: (a) $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ are perfect; (b) the isomorphisms $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$ and $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$ satisfy $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $tu_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=u_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$ for $t=\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})$ and the root $\alpha(t)=x^2$; (c) $n_\alpha=u_\alpha(1)u_{-\alpha}(-1)u_\alpha(1)=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents the nontrivial element $s_\alpha$ of $W(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$, $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$, and $s_\alpha$ acts on $X(T_2)$ by $\chi\mapsto\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ with $\alpha^\vee=\operatorname{id}$; (d) the natural surjection $\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2$ is a central isogeny with kernel $\mu_2$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is simply connected, and every automorphism of $(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$ maps $U^+$ to $U^+$ or $U^-$ and is determined by its restrictions to $T_2$ and $U^+$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a
split reductive group over a field $k$, let $B\supseteq T$ be a Borel subgroup,
and let $X(T)^+$ be the set of dominant characters of the maximal torus $T$
([[def-weight-and-dominant-weight-of-a-rational-representation]]). For every
$\lambda\in X(T)^+$ there exists a simple rational representation $V(\lambda)$
of $G$, unique up to isomorphism, whose $T$-weight decomposition is
$$V(\lambda)=V(\lambda)_\lambda\oplus\bigoplus_{\mu<\lambda}V(\lambda)_\mu$$
with $\dim_kV(\lambda)_\lambda=1$, and every simple rational representation of
$G$ is isomorphic to $V(\lambda)$ for a unique $\lambda\in X(T)^+$
([[thm-simple-rational-representations-have-a-highest-weight]],
[[thm-simple-modules-with-equal-highest-weight-are-isomorphic]],
[[lem-dominant-characters-arise-as-primitive-weights-for-split-reductive-groups]]).
The map sending a simple representation to its highest weight is a bijection
from the set of isomorphism classes of simple rational representations of $G$
to $X(T)^+$; it holds in every characteristic.

Let $k$ be a field, let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ with Weyl
group $W$ and root datum $(X,\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$, $X=X(T)$, and let
$B\supseteq T$ be a Borel subgroup with system of positive roots $\Phi^+$ and
base $\Delta$
([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]],
[[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). For a rational
representation $(V,r)$ of $G$
([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]) the
$T$-weight decomposition is $V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in X}V_\chi$ with
$V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(v)=v\otimes e_\chi\}$
([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]]); the
**weights** of $(V,r)$ are the characters $\chi$ with $V_\chi\ne0$, and
$V_\chi$ is the **weight space** of $\chi$. An element $\lambda\in X$ is
**dominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0$ for every
$\alpha\in\Phi^+$ (equivalently, for every $\alpha\in\Delta$); write $X^+$ for
the set of dominant weights. Define a partial order on $X$ by $\lambda\ge\mu$ if
and only if
$\lambda-\mu=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. The **fundamental weights** $\omega_i$
($i\in\Delta$) are the elements of $X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ dual to the
simple coroots, $\langle\omega_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle=\delta_{ij}$; they form a
basis of the weight lattice part and every $\lambda\in X\otimes\mathbb Q$
decomposes as
$\lambda=\sum_i\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\omega_i+\lambda_0$ with
$\lambda_0$ pairing to $0$ with every coroot
([[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
simple rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ with Borel
subgroup $B\supseteq T$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]], [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a)
$V$ contains a primitive vector $v$, and it is unique up to multiplication by a
nonzero scalar; (b) its weight $\lambda$ is dominant and the weight space
$V_\lambda=kv$ is one-dimensional; (c) every weight $\mu$ of $V$ satisfies
$\mu\le\lambda$, i.e. $\mu=\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\ge0$; (d) any two primitive vectors of $V$ have the same weight; this
weight is called the **highest weight** of $V$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ and let
$n\in N_G(T)(R)$ for a $k$-algebra $R$. If $v\in V_\lambda$, then $n\cdot(v\otimes1)\in(V\otimes_kR)_{n\lambda}$, where $n\lambda:T_R\to\mathbf G_{m,R}$ is the character $t\mapsto\lambda(n^{-1}tn)$, tested over every $R$-algebra. If $R$ is disconnected, this character can vary between components; the target denotes its eigensubmodule over $R$. Consequently, for every $w\in W(G,T)$ the weight spaces
$V_\lambda$ and $V_{w\lambda}$ have the same dimension, and the set of weights
of $(V,r)$ is stable under $W$
([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]],
[[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ (not necessarily
finite-dimensional) that is generated as a $G$-module by a primitive vector $v$
of weight $\lambda$
([[def-primitive-vector-of-a-rational-representation]]). Then: (a) $V$ is
generated as a module over the opposite unipotent group $U^-$ by $v$; (b)
$V=kv\oplus\bigoplus_{\mu<\lambda}V_\mu$, where every weight $\mu$ of $V$ has
the form $\mu=\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and $V_\lambda=kv$ has dimension one; (c)
$\lambda$ is dominant; (d) the sum of all proper $G$-stable subspaces of $V$ is
proper, so $V$ has a largest proper $G$-submodule and the quotient by it is a
simple $G$-module generated by the image of $v$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group, $B\supseteq T$ a Borel subgroup with
unipotent radical $U=B_u$ and roots $\Phi$
([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]],
[[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]],
[[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Let $(V,r)$ be a rational
representation
([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). A
nonzero vector $v\in V$ is **primitive** (for the pair $(B,T)$) if it spans a
$B$-stable line. Such a vector is fixed by $U$ and is a $T$-eigenvector: the action on its one-dimensional line restricts to a character of $T$, and unipotence forces the action of $U$ on that line to be trivial. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the cited split-Borel structure, the converse holds as well: a nonzero $U$-fixed $T$-eigenvector is primitive.
The **weight** of a primitive vector is the character $\lambda\in X(T)$ with
$t\cdot v=\lambda(t)v$ for all $t$ and all $k$-algebras; for a finite-dimensional
$V$ it is the weight $\lambda$ with $v\in V_\lambda$
([[def-weight-and-dominant-weight-of-a-rational-representation]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$, let $v\in V_\lambda$
be a weight vector, and let $\alpha\in\Phi$ with root-group isomorphism
$u_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\to U_\alpha$
([[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then there are vectors
$v_i\in V_{\lambda+i\alpha}$ ($i\ge1$), only finitely many nonzero, such that
$$u_\alpha(c)\cdot v=v+\sum_{i\ge1}c^i v_i$$
for every $c$ (and every $k$-algebra after base change). In particular the orbit
map $c\mapsto u_\alpha(c)\cdot v$ is polynomial with constant term $v$ and
higher coefficients in the stated weight spaces.

Let $k$ be a field and let $G$ be a diagonalizable group over $k$, so that $O(G)=k[M]$ for an abelian group $M$ with group-like basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$ ([[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then every rational representation $(V,\rho)$ of $G$ ([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]) decomposes as
$$V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in M}V_\chi,\qquad V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(v)=v\otimes e_\chi\},$$
a direct sum over the characters $\chi\in X(G)=M$ of $G$ of the corresponding eigenspaces. The eigenspaces may have arbitrary multiplicities. The decomposition is choice-free and is inherited by subrepresentations, quotients and the middle terms of extensions. In finite dimension, choosing finite bases of the nonzero eigenspaces expresses a representation as a finite direct sum of one-dimensional character representations; in particular $G$ is linearly reductive. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the same character-line decomposition holds in arbitrary dimension by [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]; only this last assertion uses arbitrary choice.

Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]) with coordinate Hopf algebra $(A,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)$ ([[def-coordinate-hopf-algebra-of-affine-group-scheme]]), and let $V$ be a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]).

(a) For a commutative unital $k$-algebra $R$ put $V_R=V\otimes_kR$ and $\operatorname{GL}_V(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]); a **rational representation** of $G$ on $V$ is a morphism of group functors $r\colon G\to\operatorname{GL}_V$, that is, a natural family of group homomorphisms $G(R)\to\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ in $R$. When $V$ is finite dimensional, a choice of basis identifies $\operatorname{GL}_V$ with the group scheme $\operatorname{GL}_n$ of [[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]].

(b) An **$A$-comodule structure** on $V$ is a $k$-linear map $\rho\colon V\to V\otimes_kA$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]) with
$$(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id}_A)\rho=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\Delta)\rho,\qquad(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\varepsilon)\rho=\operatorname{id}_V;$$
a subspace $W\subseteq V$ is a **subcomodule** if $\rho(W)\subseteq W\otimes_kA$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

(c) The two notions correspond: a comodule structure $\rho$ gives the representation by $r_R(g)(v\otimes1)=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes g)\rho(v)$, extended $R$-linearly, and this assignment is a bijection onto the rational representations of $G$ on $V$ under which subcomodules correspond to subrepresentations; the proof is [[lem-representations-of-affine-group-schemes-are-comodules]].

(d) The coaction $\Delta\colon A\to A\otimes_kA$ makes $A$ itself an $A$-comodule, the **regular representation** of $G$. A representation $r$ is **faithful** if every $r_R$ is injective.

The axioms in (b) are exactly the two comodule diagrams; no smoothness, reducedness or finite-dimensionality of $V$ is imposed, and a basis of $V$ is chosen only to name the matrix group $\operatorname{GL}_n$.

For a vector space $V$, let $J$ be the two-sided ideal of $T(V)$ generated by

$$v\otimes w-w\otimes v\qquad(v,w\in V).$$

The **symmetric algebra** of $V$ is the commutative graded algebra

$$S(V)=T(V)/J.$$

The quotient is commutative because its degree-one generators commute, and
all elements are sums of products of those generators. Since the relators are
homogeneous of degree two, $J$ is homogeneous. In degree $n$, the relation
space is generated by adjacent-transposition differences: an arbitrary
permutation difference is a telescoping sum along adjacent transpositions,
and each adjacent difference is a degree-$n$ multiple of a generator of $J$.
Thus the degree-$n$ piece is the quotient of $V^{\otimes n}$ by the span of
$t-\sigma(t)$ for $t\in V^{\otimes n}$ and $\sigma\in S_n$. The degree-zero
unit is the image of $1\in k$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]) with coordinate Hopf algebra $(A,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)$ ([[def-coordinate-hopf-algebra-of-affine-group-scheme]]), and let $V$ be a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]).

(a) For a commutative unital $k$-algebra $R$ put $V_R=V\otimes_kR$ and $\operatorname{GL}_V(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]); a **rational representation** of $G$ on $V$ is a morphism of group functors $r\colon G\to\operatorname{GL}_V$, that is, a natural family of group homomorphisms $G(R)\to\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ in $R$. When $V$ is finite dimensional, a choice of basis identifies $\operatorname{GL}_V$ with the group scheme $\operatorname{GL}_n$ of [[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]].

(b) An **$A$-comodule structure** on $V$ is a $k$-linear map $\rho\colon V\to V\otimes_kA$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]) with
$$(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id}_A)\rho=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\Delta)\rho,\qquad(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\varepsilon)\rho=\operatorname{id}_V;$$
a subspace $W\subseteq V$ is a **subcomodule** if $\rho(W)\subseteq W\otimes_kA$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

(c) The two notions correspond: a comodule structure $\rho$ gives the representation by $r_R(g)(v\otimes1)=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes g)\rho(v)$, extended $R$-linearly, and this assignment is a bijection onto the rational representations of $G$ on $V$ under which subcomodules correspond to subrepresentations; the proof is [[lem-representations-of-affine-group-schemes-are-comodules]].

(d) The coaction $\Delta\colon A\to A\otimes_kA$ makes $A$ itself an $A$-comodule, the **regular representation** of $G$. A representation $r$ is **faithful** if every $r_R$ is injective.

The axioms in (b) are exactly the two comodule diagrams; no smoothness, reducedness or finite-dimensionality of $V$ is imposed, and a basis of $V$ is chosen only to name the matrix group $\operatorname{GL}_n$.

derivations.claim: With the identification $X(T_2)=\mathbb Z\chi$ of [F1], the fundamental weight is $\omega=\chi$ and $X(T_2)^+=\{m\chi:m\ge0\}$, so [F2] gives the simple modules $L(m)=V(m\chi)$ for $m\ge0$. The trivial representation is one-dimensional hence simple with highest weight $0$, so $L(0)$ is the trivial representation. The standard representation $k^2$ is simple: for any nonzero $v=(a,b)$ one has $\binom{a\ 0}{b\ a^{-1}}e_1=v$ when $a\ne0$ and $\binom{0\ -b^{-1}}{b\ 0}e_1=v$ when $a=0$, so the submodule generated by any nonzero vector is all of $k^2$; moreover $e_1$ is fixed by $U^+$ and is a $T_2$-eigenvector of weight $\chi$, so $e_1$ is primitive of weight $\chi=\omega$ and $k^2\cong L(1)$ by [F2].

Fix $m\ge0$ and let $v\in L(m)$ be a primitive vector of weight $m\chi$, which exists and is unique up to scalar by [F3]. By [F4] $L(m)$ is generated as a $U^-$-module by $v$, and $U^-=U_{-\alpha}\cong\mathbf G_a$. By [F5] write $u_{-\alpha}(c)\cdot v=\sum_{i\ge0}c^iv_i$, where $v_0=v$, $v_i\in L(m)_{(m-2i)\chi}$, and only finitely many $v_i$ are nonzero. Let $W=\operatorname{span}_k\{v_i:i\ge0\}$. For every $k$-algebra $R$ and $a\in R$, the group law gives $u_{-\alpha}(a)\cdot(u_{-\alpha}(c)\cdot v)=u_{-\alpha}(a+c)\cdot v$; comparing coefficients of $c^j$ in these polynomial expressions yields $u_{-\alpha}(a)\cdot v_j=\sum_{i\ge j}\binom{i}{j}a^{i-j}v_i$, so $W_R$ is stable under every $U^-(R)$-point. Thus $W$ is a $U^-$-submodule containing $v$, and [F4] implies $L(m)=W$. The weights $(m-2i)\chi$ are distinct, so this is a direct sum of one-dimensional spaces $kv_i$ for the nonzero coefficients; hence every weight space of $L(m)$ has dimension at most one.

Assume now $p=\operatorname{char}(k)>0$ and put $W=ke_1^p\oplus ke_2^p\subseteq S^p(k^2)$. For $g\in\mathrm{SL}_2(R)$ with $ge_1=ae_1+ce_2$, the multinomial expansion in characteristic $p$ gives $g\cdot e_1^p=(ae_1+ce_2)^p=a^pe_1^p+c^pe_2^p\in W_R$, and likewise $g\cdot e_2^p=(be_1+de_2)^p=b^pe_1^p+d^pe_2^p\in W_R$; thus $W$ is a $G$-submodule of $S^p(k^2)$, of dimension two because $e_1^p,e_2^p$ are distinct basis monomials. The same computation is the identity $g\cdot e_i^p=(g\cdot e_i)^p$.

If $v_i\ne0$, then $(m-2i)\chi$ is a weight of $L(m)$, so by the Weyl-group stability of [F3] and $s_\alpha(\chi)=-\chi$ of [F1], the character $(2i-m)\chi$ is again a weight; by [F3] applied to $L(m)$ it has the form $(m-2j)\chi$ with $j\ge0$, so $2i-m=m-2j$, that is $i+j=m$ and $0\le i\le m$. Hence at most $m+1$ of the vectors $v_i$ are nonzero and $\dim_kL(m)\le m+1$; every weight other than $m\chi$ lies in $\{(m-2)\chi,\dots,-m\chi\}$ with multiplicity at most one.

The submodule $W$ is $T_2$-stable with weight spaces $ke_1^p$ of weight $p\chi$ and $ke_2^p$ of weight $-p\chi$. Let $S\subseteq W$ be a nonzero submodule; by [F6] $S$ contains a nonzero weight vector, hence a nonzero multiple of $e_1^p$ or of $e_2^p$. If $e_1^p\in S$, then $u_{-\alpha}(1)\cdot e_1^p=e_1^p+e_2^p\in S$ and hence $e_2^p\in S$; if $e_2^p\in S$, then $u_\alpha(1)\cdot e_2^p=e_2^p+e_1^p\in S$ and hence $e_1^p\in S$. In both cases $S=W$, so $W$ is simple.

Finally $e_1^p$ is fixed by $U^+$ and is a $T_2$-eigenvector of weight $p\chi$, so it is a primitive vector of weight $p\chi$ in the simple module $W$; the submodule it generates is contained in $W$ by step 1.3 and contains it by step 2.2, so it is all of $W$, and $p\chi$ is dominant. By the classification [F2] the simple module with highest weight $p\chi=p\omega$ is $L(p)$, whence $W\cong L(p)$. In the basis $e_1^p,e_2^p$ of $W$, step 1.3 gives the entrywise $p$-th powers of the standard representation matrices. These are the action matrices of the Frobenius twist $L(1)^{(p)}$. The $k$-linear map sending its two basis vectors to $e_1^p,e_2^p$ is therefore a $G$-module isomorphism onto $W$, over every field $k$ of characteristic $p$.
